The bootstrap's performance in this cell is the simulation counterpart of the cluster-robust bootstrap we rely on for Table 2.", aca_bias_wt, aca_rmse_wt, aca_tau_wt, 100 * aca_cov_boot, 100 * aca_cov_jk, 100 * aca_cov_plac)`

`r if (mc_available && !mc_has_aca) "*The ACA-calibrated configuration described in Section 4.1 is not present in this build's* \\texttt{mc\\_results.csv}*; re-running* \\texttt{scripts/run\\_mc\\_simulations.R} *computes it (the completed grid configurations are skipped) and adds its row to the tables.*"`

```{r mc-trend-run, cache=FALSE}
## Trend cell (Section 4.1): a size-correlated trend added to L. Diagnosis only
## --- shows the population-weighted estimators inherit bias and the in-time
## placebo detects it. Generated by scripts/run_mc_trend.R (no remedy columns:
## the paper's use of this cell is diagnostic, not a remedy horse-race).
mc_trend_available <- file.exists(file.path("data", "mc_trend_results.csv"))
mc_trend_df <- if (mc_trend_available) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path("data", "mc_trend_results.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
} else NULL
```

`r if (mc_trend_available) "Table \\ref{tab:mc-trend} isolates the mechanism behind the application's placebo failure. A size-correlated trend leaves the equally-weighted estimator unbiased for its target but induces a growing bias in both the population-weighted SDID and the population-weighted DID estimators---the bias travels with the weights, not the estimator---while the in-time placebo, which is zero in expectation absent a trend, grows with $\\gamma_{\\text{trend}}$ and so detects it. This is the simulation counterpart of Section 3.6: a differential trend that loads on the largest units contaminates the population-weighted target under any level-matched design, and the estimand-specific placebo is what surfaces it."`

```{r mc-trend-table, eval=mc_trend_available}
trend_tbl <- mc_trend_df %>%
  group_by(gamma_trend) %>%
  summarise(
    Bias_eq      = mean(est_sdid_eq - true_att_equal,    na.rm = TRUE),
    Bias_sdid_wt = mean(est_sdid_wt - true_att_weighted, na.rm = TRUE),
    Bias_did_wt  = mean(est_did_wt  - true_att_weighted, na.rm = TRUE),
    Placebo_wt   = mean(est_plac_wt,                     na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(-gamma_trend, ~ round(., 3)))

kableExtra::kbl(
  trend_tbl, booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "Monte Carlo: a size-correlated trend biases the population-weighted estimators and is detected by the in-time placebo.",
  label = "mc-trend",
  col.names = c("$\\gamma_{\\text{trend}}$", "Bias (eq.)",
                "Bias (pop., SDID)", "Bias (pop., DID)", "In-time placebo"),
  escape = FALSE, align = c("r", "r", "r", "r", "r")
) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position")) %>%
  kableExtra::footnote(
    general = "200 simulations per cell at $N_1 = 20$, $\\\\gamma = 0.5$, and moderate weight concentration (HHI $= 0.15$). Bias is computed against each estimator's own target ATT; the population-weighted target is held fixed across cells (the trend perturbs the factor structure $L$, not the treatment effect). The final column is the mean in-time placebo estimate under population weights, which is zero in expectation when $\\\\gamma_{\\\\text{trend}} = 0$. Detrended and stratified variants are omitted here and reported in the supplementary appendix.",
    general_title = "Notes:", threeparttable = TRUE, escape = FALSE)
```


# Discussion

We have shown that the SDID estimator of @arkhangelsky2021 admits a parsimonious extension to incorporate researcher-specified weights on treated units, with consistency and asymptotic normality results that inherit from the underlying factor-model framework subject to a no-dominant-weight regularity condition. We have also documented, through both formal characterization and direct application, that this regularity condition loses its practical bite in many policy settings, particularly those involving population weights on heterogeneously sized geographic units. In such settings, plug-in asymptotic standard errors are unreliable; cluster-robust bootstrap inference at a level of aggregation where the no-dominant-cluster condition is plausible is the appropriate finite-sample tool. Our application provides a concrete illustration: with $N_1^{\text{eff}} \approx `r round(n1_eff, 0)`$ and one county carrying $\approx `r round(top1_share * 100, 1)`\%$ of total weight, the asymptotic approximation cannot be trusted at face value, but state-level cluster bootstrapping across the `r n_states_treated` treated state clusters, complemented by randomization inference, provides a defensible alternative.

The ACA application illustrates more than the technical contribution. The equally-weighted and population-weighted estimands diverge by `r round(abs(as.numeric(tau_sdid_w) - as.numeric(tau_sdid)), 0)` deaths per 100,000---enough to swing the qualitative interpretation of the policy from "no detectable effect" to "substantial mortality reduction." The in-time placebo of Section 3.6 shows that the population-weighted *level* is not credibly identified in this county design: it loads on a size-correlated differential mortality trend that convex, level-matched estimators cannot remove, and the same falsification would challenge any level-matched population-weighted design on this panel, including the published benchmark. This is a property of the ACA county setting, not of the weighting; the recent triple-difference and administrative-data literature is built precisely to identify the population-scaled mortality effects that a single-difference county design cannot [@miller2021; @wyse2025]. What survives regardless is the paper's central point: the equally-weighted target is a clean, precisely-estimated null, so the *divergence* between estimands is real whatever the true population-weighted magnitude proves to be. The choice between these estimands is not a statistical matter but a substantive one. A researcher interested in the average effect across counties as administrative units might reasonably prefer equal weighting; a researcher interested in the per-capita effect on the population exposed to expanded Medicaid coverage, as is the natural reading for cost-benefit and welfare calculations, should prefer population weighting. Both estimands are well-defined and identifiable; the published mortality literature has implicitly favored the population-weighted target through cluster sampling, propensity-score weighting, or other means [@borgschulte2020; @miller2021]. Our contribution makes this choice transparent and provides a tool that respects it directly.

Three caveats merit discussion. First, our treated-unit weights are fixed by the researcher rather than estimated. We do not claim optimality in any decision-theoretic sense; the weights encode the researcher's definition of the estimand. Adapting the weights to optimally estimate a target subpopulation effect (in the spirit of @hirano2003 for propensity-score weighting) is a natural extension we leave for future work. Second, while we provide cluster-robust bootstrap and jackknife inference, our adaptation of the placebo variance estimator uses uniform weights for pseudo-treated units, which may understate variance when treatment effects are highly heterogeneous; the implications for finite-sample coverage are examined in the companion supplement. Third, our main development and application assume simultaneous adoption. Section 2.5 sketches the extension to staggered settings---cohort-wise weighted estimation against not-yet-treated controls, aggregated with researcher-chosen cohort weights, implemented in the software and formalized in the supplement---but we do not pursue a staggered application here. The interaction between within-cohort and across-cohort weighting connects naturally to the broader literature on aggregation in heterogeneous-effects panel designs [@callaway2021; @sun2021; @dechaisemartin2020], and a substantive staggered application is left to future work.

\section*{Data availability}

Data used in this study are publicly available from CDC WONDER (mortality, Underlying Cause of Death file, all-cause mortality among adults aged 20--64, ICD-10 codes A00--Y89; county-year cells with 1--9 deaths are suppressed in the public file and are imputed by allocating exact state-year residuals, as described in Supplementary Appendix E.5) [@cdcwonder]; the SEER program (county-level population by age and sex) [@seer]; and the Bureau of Labor Statistics (county-level unemployment, Local Area Unemployment Statistics) [@bls_laus]. The BV reproduction in Supplementary Appendix E.5 additionally uses the ACS 2009--2013 5-year file and Census SAHIE 2013 (via the Census API), and county presidential returns from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab. Replication code, the weighted \texttt{synthdid} R package extension, and a companion supplementary appendix containing full proofs of Propositions 1--3, synthetic-control diagnostics, alternative weight specifications, leave-one-out sensitivity, and a complete description of the DLPS implementation are available at \url{https://github.com/johniselin-econ/synthdid_weights}.
